flashcards.title: Nature of Physics
explanation: Physics: A branch of science that deals with the study of the natural world, including matter, energy, and their interactions.
Objective: To understand the laws of nature and apply them to explain and predict natural phenomena.
Examples: Laws of motion, thermodynamics, gravitation, optics, etc.

flashcards.title: Scope of Physics
explanation: Macroscopic Level: Deals with phenomena at large scales, like planetary motion, fluids, thermodynamics.
Microscopic Level: Deals with atomic and subatomic phenomena, like quantum mechanics, nuclear physics.
Interdisciplinary: Physics contributes to chemistry (quantum chemistry), biology (biophysics), geology (geophysics), etc.

flashcards.title: Fundamental Forces in Nature
explanation: Gravitational Force: Weakest force but acts over infinite range; governs planetary motion and tides.
Electromagnetic Force: Acts between charged particles; responsible for electric and magnetic phenomena.
Strong Nuclear Force: Strongest force; binds protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Weak Nuclear Force: Responsible for radioactive decay and certain nuclear reactions.

flashcards.title: Unification and Reductionism
explanation: Unification: Explaining diverse phenomena using a single set of laws (e.g., Maxwell's equations for electromagnetism).
Reductionism: Breaking down complex systems into simpler components for better understanding (e.g., understanding matter at atomic levels).

flashcards.title: Scientific Method
explanation: Steps: Observation → Hypothesis → Experiment → Theory → Law.
Empirical Basis: Scientific theories and laws are based on experimental evidence.
Predictability: Theories should predict phenomena and be falsifiable.

flashcards.title: Relation of Physics with Other Disciplines
explanation: Physics and Chemistry: Atomic structure, spectroscopy, and chemical bonding.
Physics and Biology: Biophysics studies biological systems using physical principles.
Physics and Astronomy: Astrophysics studies celestial objects using physics principles.

flashcards.title: Technology and Society
explanation: Technological Advances: Physics has led to inventions like computers, satellites, nuclear energy, and medical imaging.
Impact on Society: Physics-based technologies have transformed transportation, communication, and healthcare.

flashcards.title: Fundamental and Derived Units
explanation: Fundamental Units: Basic units of measurement (e.g., meter, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela).
Derived Units: Units derived from fundamental units (e.g., velocity in m/s, force in N = kg·m/s²).
SI Units: International System of Units is the standardized unit system used globally.

flashcards.title: Dimensional Analysis
explanation: Dimensional Formula: Expresses a physical quantity in terms of fundamental dimensions (Mass [M], Length [L], Time [T]).
Applications: To check dimensional consistency, derive relations, and convert units.

flashcards.title: Measurement of Length, Mass, and Time
explanation: Length: Measured using tools like meter scales, Vernier calipers, and screw gauges.
Mass: Measured using beam balances or electronic balances.
Time: Measured using mechanical clocks, digital clocks, and atomic clocks (high precision).

flashcards.title: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors
explanation: Accuracy: Closeness of a measured value to the true value.
Precision: Closeness of repeated measurements to each other.
Errors: Differences between the measured and true value (Systematic Error, Random Error).

flashcards.title: Significant Figures
explanation: Significant Figures: Digits in a number that carry meaningful contributions to its measurement accuracy.
Rules: Non-zero digits are always significant. Zeros between significant digits are significant. Leading zeros are not significant.

flashcards.title: Rounding Off Numbers
explanation: Rules: If the digit to be dropped is less than 5, leave the preceding digit unchanged. If the digit to be dropped is 5 or greater, increase the preceding digit by 1.

flashcards.title: Combination of Errors
formulas: Error in Sum/Difference: ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB
Error in Product/Quotient: ΔZ / Z = (ΔA / A) + (ΔB / B)
Error in Powers: ΔZ / Z = n(ΔA / A)
explanation: Sum/Difference: Errors are added in absolute terms.
Product/Quotient: Errors are added in relative terms.
Powers: Errors are multiplied by the power of the quantity.

flashcards.title: Applications of Dimensional Analysis
explanation: Checking Consistency: Dimensional analysis helps verify the correctness of equations.
Deriving Relations: Used to derive formulas by equating dimensions on both sides.
Unit Conversion: Helps convert physical quantities from one unit system to another.

flashcards.title: Basics of Motion
explanation: Position: The location of an object relative to a reference point.
Path Length: Total distance traveled by an object irrespective of direction.
Displacement: The shortest distance between the initial and final positions; a vector quantity.

flashcards.title: Average and Instantaneous Quantities
formulas: Average Speed: speed_avg = total distance / total time
explanation: Average Velocity: Total displacement divided by total time.
Average Speed: Total path length divided by total time.
Instantaneous Velocity: Velocity at a specific instant of time.
Instantaneous Acceleration: Acceleration at a specific instant of time.

flashcards.title: Equations of Motion for Uniform Acceleration
explanation: These equations describe the motion of an object under constant acceleration.
u: Initial velocity, v: Final velocity, a: Acceleration, x: Displacement, t: Time.

flashcards.title: Graphical Representation of Motion
explanation: Position-Time Graph: Slope of the graph gives velocity.
Velocity-Time Graph: Slope of the graph gives acceleration; area under the graph gives displacement.
Acceleration-Time Graph: Area under the graph gives change in velocity.

flashcards.title: Relative Motion
explanation: Relative Velocity: The velocity of an object (A) relative to another object (B) is given by v_AB = v_A - v_B.
Relative motion helps compare the motion of two objects in the same or opposite directions.

flashcards.title: Uniform and Non-Uniform Motion
explanation: Uniform Motion: Motion with constant velocity (a = 0).
Non-Uniform Motion: Motion with changing velocity; acceleration is non-zero.

flashcards.title: Free Fall Motion
explanation: Free Fall: Motion of an object under the influence of gravity alone.
Acceleration due to gravity (g): Approximately 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface.

flashcards.title: Key Differences between Distance and Displacement
explanation: Distance: Scalar quantity; total path traveled.
Displacement: Vector quantity; shortest distance between initial and final positions.
Distance is always positive, while displacement can be positive, negative, or zero.

flashcards.title: Basics of Vector Quantities
explanation: Scalars: Quantities that have only magnitude (e.g., mass, time, speed).
Vectors: Quantities that have both magnitude and direction (e.g., displacement, velocity, force).
Representation: A vector is represented by an arrow; length represents magnitude, and arrowhead represents direction.

flashcards.title: Addition and Subtraction of Vectors
formulas: Resultant Vector: R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)
Direction: tan θ = (B sin θ) / (A + B cos θ)
explanation: Addition of Vectors: Using the triangle or parallelogram law.
Subtraction of Vectors: Adding the negative of a vector (reverse its direction).
Resultant Vector: Magnitude and direction are calculated using trigonometry.

flashcards.title: Resolution of Vectors
explanation: Resolution: Breaking a vector into components along mutually perpendicular directions.
Components: Horizontal (A_x = A cos θ) and vertical (A_y = A sin θ).
Applications: Simplifies vector addition and other calculations.

flashcards.title: Projectile Motion
formulas: Time of Flight: T = (2u sin θ) / g
explanation: Projectile Motion: Motion of an object under gravity with an initial velocity at an angle θ.
Time of Flight: Total time the projectile remains in the air.
Maximum Height: The highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
Horizontal Range: The total horizontal distance covered by the projectile.

flashcards.title: Uniform Circular Motion
explanation: Uniform Circular Motion: Motion of an object in a circular path with constant speed.
Centripetal Force: Force acting towards the center of the circle, required to keep the object in circular motion.
Angular Velocity: Rate of change of angular displacement.

flashcards.title: Relative Motion in Two Dimensions
explanation: Relative Velocity: The velocity of an object A relative to another object B.
In Two Dimensions: Components of velocities are subtracted separately along each axis.

flashcards.title: Motion Under Gravity in Two Dimensions
explanation: Horizontal Motion: Uniform motion with constant velocity, x = u_x t.
Vertical Motion: Accelerated motion under gravity, y = u_y t - (1/2) g t².
Velocity Components: v_x remains constant, v_y changes due to gravity.

flashcards.title: Displacement in Two Dimensions
explanation: Resultant Displacement: R = √(x² + y²), where x and y are components of displacement.
Direction: Angle θ of the resultant vector is given by tan θ = y / x.

flashcards.title: Newton's Laws and Impulse
explanation: Newton's First Law: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force.
Newton's Second Law: The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the applied force, F = ma.
Impulse: The product of force and time, which equals the change in momentum, Impulse = FΔt = Δp.

flashcards.title: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Momentum
explanation: Newton's Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction, F₁₂ = -F₂₁.
Conservation of Linear Momentum: The total momentum of a system remains constant in the absence of external forces.
Equilibrium: For a body in equilibrium, ΣF = 0.

flashcards.title: Points to Note on Frames of Reference
explanation: Non-Inertial Frame: An accelerated frame where pseudo-forces need to be introduced.
Weight Apparent in a Lift: Moving upward (W = m(g + a)), Moving downward (W = m(g - a)).
Newton's Laws: Valid only in inertial frames.

flashcards.title: Friction and Its Types
explanation: Kinetic Friction: Force opposing relative motion, fₖ = μₖN.
Static Friction: Maximum force before motion begins, fₛ(max) = μₛN.
Friction: Acts between surfaces in contact, opposing relative motion.

flashcards.title: Inertial and Non-Inertial Frames of Reference
explanation: Inertial Frame: A frame where objects move with constant velocity, and Newton's laws are valid.
Non-Inertial Frame: A frame with acceleration where pseudo-forces are required to apply Newton's laws.

flashcards.title: Work
explanation: Work: Defined as the dot product of force and displacement. For constant force, W = F · s, where F is force and s is displacement.
For variable force: Work is given by dW = F · ds.

flashcards.title: Conservative and Non-Conservative Forces
explanation: Conservative Forces: Work done in a closed path is zero (e.g., gravitational force, electrical force).
Non-Conservative Forces: Work done depends on the path taken (e.g., friction).

flashcards.title: Kinetic and Potential Energy
explanation: Kinetic Energy: Energy possessed by a body due to motion, KE = (1/2)mv².
Work-Energy Theorem: Net work done by external forces equals the change in kinetic energy, W = Kf - Ki.
Potential Energy: Energy due to configuration or position, ΔU = -∫F · dr.

flashcards.title: Power and Conservation of Energy
formulas: KE₁ + PE₁ + Eₑₓₜ = KE₂ + PE₂ + Eₑₓₜ
explanation: Power: Rate of doing work, given by P = F · v, where F is force and v is velocity.
Conservation of Energy: Total energy remains constant in the absence of external forces, KE₁ + PE₁ + Eₑₓₜ = KE₂ + PE₂ + Eₑₓₜ.

flashcards.title: Linear Momentum and Collisions
explanation: Linear Momentum: Product of mass and velocity, p = mv.
Impulse-Momentum Theorem: Change in momentum is equal to impulse, FΔt = Δp.
Conservation of Momentum: Total momentum before and after collision remains constant, Σpₐ = Σpₓ.

flashcards.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
explanation: Elastic Collisions: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
Inelastic Collisions: Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not.

flashcards.title: Special Cases of Elastic Collisions
explanation: When m₁ = m₂: Velocities are exchanged after collision.
When m₂ is at rest: Final velocities depend on the mass ratio and initial velocity of m₁.

chapters.name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

flashcards.title: Mechanics of System of Particles
explanation: Centre of Mass (Rₒ): The point where the entire mass of the system can be assumed to be concentrated.
Velocity of Centre of Mass (vₒ): The total momentum of a system of particles is equal to the total mass times the velocity of the centre of mass.
Momentum Conservation: The total momentum in the motion of the centre of mass is conserved if no external force acts on the system.

flashcards.title: Rigid Body Dynamics - Angular Variables
explanation: Angular Displacement (θ): The angle swept by a body about a fixed axis.
Angular Velocity (ω): The rate of change of angular displacement, ω = dθ/dt.
Angular Acceleration (α): The rate of change of angular velocity, α = dω/dt.

flashcards.title: Moment of Inertia and Torque
explanation: Moment of Inertia (I): The rotational analog of mass, depends on the mass distribution relative to the axis of rotation.
Torque (τ): The rotational analog of force, τ = r × F.
Relation Between Torque and Angular Acceleration: τ = Iα.

flashcards.title: Rotational Energy and Work
explanation: Rotational Kinetic Energy (KEᵣₒₜ): Energy due to rotation, given by KEᵣₒₜ = (1/2)Iω².
Rotational Work Done (W): Work done by torque over an angular displacement, W = τθ.

flashcards.title: Angular Momentum and Its Conservation
explanation: Angular Momentum (L): Product of moment of inertia and angular velocity, L = Iω.
Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum: If the external torque is zero, the angular momentum of the system remains constant.

flashcards.title: Pure Rolling Motion
explanation: Pure Rolling: A combination of rotational and translational motion where v = rω.
Total Energy in Rolling Motion (Eₑ): Sum of translational and rotational kinetic energy, Eₑ = (1/2)mv² + (1/2)Iω² + mgh.

flashcards.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation and Acceleration Due to Gravity
explanation: Newton's Law of Gravitation: The force between two masses is proportional to their product and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
Acceleration Due to Gravity (g): At the Earth's surface, g is given by g = GM / R², where G is the gravitational constant, M is Earth's mass, and R is Earth's radius.

flashcards.title: Gravitational Potential Energy and Potential
explanation: Gravitational Potential Energy: The potential energy of a mass m at a height h above the Earth's surface is given by PE = -GMm / (R + h).
Gravitational Potential (V): The potential at a height h is V = -GM / (R + h).

flashcards.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
explanation: Law of Orbits: Every planet revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus.
Law of Areas: A line joining the planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals.
Law of Periods: The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its mean distance from the Sun, T² ∝ R³.

flashcards.title: Escape Velocity and Satellites
explanation: Escape Velocity (vₑ): The minimum velocity required to escape Earth's gravitational field is vₑ = √(2GM / R) or vₑ = √(2gR).
Orbital Velocity (vₒ): The velocity needed for a satellite to orbit Earth is vₒ = √(gR).
Period of Satellites: The time period of a satellite in orbit is T = 2π √[(R + h)³ / gR²].

flashcards.title: Variation of g with Altitude, Depth, and Latitude
explanation: With Altitude (gₐ): g decreases as the altitude (h) increases, gₐ = g(1 - 2h / R).
With Depth (gₓ): g decreases linearly with depth (d), gₓ = g(1 - d / R).
With Latitude (gₗ): g varies due to the Earth's rotation, gₗ = g - 0.037cos²ϕ.

flashcards.title: Elasticity and Stress
explanation: Elasticity: The ability of a body to regain its original shape and size when deforming force is removed.
Stress: Force applied per unit area, Stress = F / A, where F is the applied force and A is the area of cross-section.

flashcards.title: Strain and Types
explanation: Strain: The ratio of change in dimension to the original dimension. It is a dimensionless quantity.
Longitudinal Strain: Change in length per unit original length.
Volume Strain: Change in volume per unit original volume.
Shear Strain: Change in shape caused by shear stress.

flashcards.title: Hook's Law and Elastic Moduli
explanation: Hook's Law: Within elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain.
Young's Modulus (Y): Ratio of tensile stress to longitudinal strain.
Bulk Modulus (K): Ratio of volume stress to volume strain.
Modulus of Rigidity (n): Ratio of shear stress to shear strain.

flashcards.title: Poisson's Ratio
explanation: Poisson's Ratio (σ): The ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain, constant for a given material.

flashcards.title: Strain Energy
explanation: Strain Energy: Energy stored per unit volume in a strained body, given by E = ½ × Stress × Strain.

flashcards.title: Hydrostatics: Pressure and Principles
explanation: Fluid Pressure: The force exerted normally on a unit area, given by P = F / A.
Hydrostatic Pressure: Pressure at depth in a fluid, P = ρgh, where ρ is density, g is gravity, and h is depth.
Gauge Pressure: Total pressure in a fluid, P = P₀ + ρgh, where P₀ is atmospheric pressure.

flashcards.title: Archimedes' Principle and Upthrust
explanation: Archimedes' Principle: A body submerged in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid.
Upthrust: The weight of the displaced liquid determines the buoyant force acting on the body.

flashcards.title: Gas Laws
explanation: Boyle's Law: For a constant temperature, the product of pressure and volume is constant (PV = constant).
Charles' Law: For a constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its temperature (V / T = constant).

flashcards.title: Hydrodynamics: Flow and Principles
explanation: Bernoulli’s Principle: The sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy, and potential energy per unit volume is constant for streamline flow.
Continuity Equation: For an incompressible fluid, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, where A is the cross-sectional area and v is the velocity.

flashcards.title: Viscosity and Stokes' Law
explanation: Viscosity: Viscous force between fluid layers, F = -ηA (dv / dx), where η is the coefficient of viscosity.
Stokes' Law: Viscous force on a spherical body, F = 6πηrv, where r is the radius and v is velocity.

flashcards.title: Poiseuille's Equation
explanation: Poiseuille's Equation: The volume of liquid flowing through a capillary tube per second, Q = (πr⁴ΔP) / (8ηl), where r is radius, ΔP is pressure difference, and l is length.

flashcards.title: Thermal Expansion
explanation: Coefficient of Linear Expansion (α): Change in length per unit length per degree rise in temperature, α = (l₂ - l₁) / (l₁ΔT).
Length at Temperature t (lₜ): lₜ = l₀(1 + αt), where l₀ is the length at 0°C.
Coefficient of Superficial Expansion (β): β = ΔA / A₀ΔT, relates area change with temperature.
Coefficient of Volume Expansion (γ): γ = ΔV / V₀ΔT, relates volume change with temperature.

flashcards.title: Measurement of Heat and Temperature
explanation: Temperature Conversion: Celsius (C), Fahrenheit (F), and Kelvin (K) scales are related by C = (F - 32) * (5 / 9) and K = C + 273.
Principle of Electrical Resistance: Rₜ = R₀(1 + αt), where Rₜ is resistance at temperature t°C.
Joule's Mechanical Equivalent of Heat (J): J = 4.2 J/cal.
Specific Heat: Heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass by 1°C.

flashcards.title: Heat Transfer
explanation: Thermal Conductivity (H): Rate of heat flow through a slab is H = kA(T₁ - T₂) / L, where k is the conductivity constant.
Stefan-Boltzmann Law: Power radiated per unit area, uₑₘ = σT⁴, where σ is Stefan's constant.
Newton’s Law of Cooling: The rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference, dt/dt = -bA(T - Tₛ).

flashcards.title: Latent Heat and Calorimetry
explanation: Latent Heat: Energy required to change the state of unit mass without temperature change, Q = mL.
Principle of Calorimetry: Heat lost by a hot body equals the heat gained by a cold body.

flashcards.title: Radiation and Kirchoff's Law
explanation: Kirchoff’s Law: The emissive power of a body is equal to its absorptive power for the same wavelength and temperature.
Emissivity (e): Ratio of energy emitted to that of a perfect blackbody.

flashcards.title: Thermodynamic States and Laws
explanation: Thermodynamic State: Defined by pressure, volume, and temperature of the system.
Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics: If two systems are in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in equilibrium with each other.
First Law of Thermodynamics: Heat energy given to the system equals the increase in internal energy and work done, Q = ΔU + W.
Second Law of Thermodynamics: Heat cannot flow from a colder body to a hotter body without external work being done.

flashcards.title: Work in Volume Changes and Processes
explanation: Work in Volume Changes: Work done when pressure remains constant, W = P(V₂ - V₁).
Isothermal Process: Temperature remains constant; W = nRT ln(V₂ / V₁).
Adiabatic Process: No heat transfer, PVᵧ = constant.

flashcards.title: Quasi-Static and Isochoric Processes
explanation: Quasi-Static Processes: System remains infinitesimally close to equilibrium throughout.
Isochoric Process: Volume remains constant, ΔU = Q.

flashcards.title: Thermal Efficiency and Heat Engines
explanation: Thermal Efficiency of Heat Engine: Efficiency is η = 1 - (Q₂ / Q₁), where Q₁ is heat absorbed and Q₂ is heat rejected.
Coefficient of Performance (COP) of Refrigerator: COP is β = Q₂ / W = Q₂ / (Q₁ - Q₂).

flashcards.title: Carnot Theorem and Efficiency
explanation: Carnot's Theorem: No engine operating between two temperatures can be more efficient than a Carnot engine.
Efficiency of Carnot Engine: Depends only on the source and sink temperatures, not on the working substance.

flashcards.title: Gas Laws
explanation: Boyle's Law: At constant temperature, the volume of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to pressure.
Charles' Law: At constant pressure, the volume of a given mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.
Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures: Total pressure of a mixture of ideal gases is the sum of the partial pressures of the individual gases.

flashcards.title: Ideal Gas Equation
explanation: Ideal Gas Equation: Relates pressure (P), volume (V), number of moles (n), gas constant (R), and temperature (T).

flashcards.title: Pressure of Gas
explanation: Pressure of Gas: The pressure exerted by a gas is related to its density (ρ) and mean square speed (vₘₛ²).
Alternate Form: P = (1/3)Nmvₘₛ², where N is the number of molecules and m is the mass of each molecule.

flashcards.title: Root Mean Square (RMS) Speed
explanation: RMS Speed: The square root of the average of the squares of the velocities of gas molecules.
Alternate Form: vₘₛ = √(3RT / M), where M is molar mass.

flashcards.title: Law of Equipartition of Energy
explanation: Law of Equipartition: Each degree of freedom has an average energy of (1/2)kT, where k is Boltzmann constant.

flashcards.title: Specific Heat Capacity
explanation: Specific Heat Capacity of Monatomic Gases: Cᵥ = (3/2)R, Cₚ = (5/2)R.
Specific Heat Capacity of Diatomic Gases: Cᵥ = (5/2)R, Cₚ = (7/2)R.

flashcards.title: Mean Free Path
explanation: Mean Free Path (λ): The average distance traveled by a molecule between successive collisions.
Alternate Form: λ = 1 / (nσ), where n is the number density and σ is the collision cross-section.

flashcards.title: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)
explanation: SHM: Restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium, F = -kx, where k is the force constant.
Differential Equation of SHM: The solution is x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), representing sinusoidal motion.

flashcards.title: Amplitude, Time Period, and Frequency
explanation: Amplitude (A): The maximum displacement of the system from equilibrium.
Time Period (T): Time taken to complete one oscillation, T = 2π / ω.
Frequency (f): Number of oscillations per unit time, f = 1 / T.

flashcards.title: Velocity and Acceleration in SHM
explanation: Velocity (v): Velocity of a particle in SHM varies as v = -Aω sin(ωt + φ).
Acceleration (a): Acceleration is proportional to displacement but in the opposite direction, a = -ω²x.

flashcards.title: Energy in SHM
explanation: Kinetic Energy (KE): Energy associated with motion, KE = (1/2)mω²(A² - x²).
Potential Energy (PE): Energy associated with position, PE = (1/2)mω²x².
Total Energy (TE): Sum of kinetic and potential energy, TE = (1/2)mω²A².

flashcards.title: Oscillations of a Spring-Mass System
explanation: Spring-Mass System: Oscillates under Hooke's Law, with time period T = 2π √(m / k), where k is the spring constant.

flashcards.title: Simple and Compound Pendulum
explanation: Simple Pendulum: Time period depends only on length and gravity, T = 2π √(l / g).
Compound Pendulum: Time period depends on moment of inertia and center of suspension, T = 2π √(I / mgl).

flashcards.title: Damped and Forced Oscillations
explanation: Damped Oscillation: Amplitude of oscillation decreases over time due to dissipative forces like friction.
Forced Oscillation and Resonance: If an external periodic force matches the natural frequency, resonance occurs.

flashcards.title: Introduction to Waves
explanation: Wave: A disturbance that travels through a medium due to periodic motion of particles. Examples: sound waves, light waves.
Mechanical Waves: Require a material medium for propagation. Examples: sound waves, water waves.
Non-Mechanical Waves: Do not require a material medium. Examples: light waves, X-rays, radio waves.

flashcards.title: Types of Waves
explanation: Transverse Waves: Displacement of particles is perpendicular to wave propagation. Example: water waves.
Longitudinal Waves: Displacement of particles is parallel to wave propagation. Example: sound waves.

flashcards.title: Wave Equations and Properties
explanation: Wave Equation: Describes displacement y at position x and time t, y(x,t) = A sin(ωt - kx).
Wave Number (k): k = 2π / λ, where λ is wavelength.
Time Period (T): Time taken for one complete oscillation, T = 1 / f.
Speed of Wave: v = λf, where f is frequency.

flashcards.title: Speed of Waves
explanation: Speed of Transverse Waves: Depends on tension (T) and linear mass density (μ), v = √(T / μ).
Speed of Longitudinal Waves: Depends on bulk modulus (B) and density (ρ), v = √(B / ρ).

flashcards.title: Principle of Superposition and Interference
explanation: Superposition Principle: When two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the sum of individual displacements.
Interference: Two waves of same frequency interfere constructively or destructively depending on phase difference (φ).

flashcards.title: Reflection and Standing Waves
explanation: Reflection of Waves: At a boundary, waves are reflected either in phase (open boundary) or out of phase (rigid boundary).
Standing Waves: Formed due to superposition of two waves traveling in opposite directions.

flashcards.title: Normal Modes and Beats
explanation: Normal Modes: Frequencies of vibration in a stretched string are integral multiples of the fundamental frequency, fₙ = n(v / 2L).
Beats: Interference between two waves of slightly different frequencies, f_beat = |f₁ - f₂|.

flashcards.title: Doppler Effect
explanation: Doppler Effect: Change in observed frequency due to relative motion of source and observer.
Formula: f' = f(v + v₀) / (v - vₛ), where v₀ is observer's velocity and vₛ is source's velocity.

flashcards.title: Charge and Coulomb's Law
explanation: Quantisation: q = n * e, where n = 0, 1, 2, ... and e is the charge of an electron (e = -1.6 * 10^-19 C).
Additivity: Total charge q(net) is the algebraic sum of individual charges.
Conservation: The total charge of an isolated system remains constant.
Coulomb's Law: The electrostatic force between two charges q1 and q2 separated by a distance r is given by F = k * (q1 * q2) / r^2.
Principle of Superposition: The net force acting on a charge is the vector sum of forces due to other charges.

flashcards.title: Electric Field and Intensity
explanation: Electric Field: The force experienced per unit positive test charge at a point, given by E = F / q0.
Electric field due to a point charge: E = k * (q / r^2).
Electric Field Intensity: It is the vector sum of electric fields due to all charges at a point.
Principle of Superposition applies to calculate the net electric field intensity.

flashcards.title: Charge Density and Electric Flux
explanation: Linear charge density (λ): Charge per unit length.
Surface charge density (σ): Charge per unit area.
Volume charge density (ρ): Charge per unit volume.
Electric Flux (Φ): The measure of electric field passing through a surface. Φ = E · A * cosθ, where θ is the angle between the field and the surface normal.

flashcards.title: Gauss's Theorem and Electrostatics in Conductors
explanation: Gauss's Theorem: The total electric flux through a closed surface equals the charge enclosed divided by the permittivity of the medium.
Electrostatics in Conductors: Electric field inside a conductor is zero in electrostatic equilibrium, and all charge resides on the outer surface of the conductor.

flashcards.title: Electric Potential and Potential Energy
explanation: Electric potential energy (U) is the work done to move charges against the electric field.
For a system of two charges: U = (1 / 4πε₀) * (q1 * q2 / r).
Electric potential (V) is the work done per unit charge to move a test charge to a point.
For a point charge: V = (1 / 4πε₀) * (q / r).

flashcards.title: Electric Dipole
explanation: An electric dipole consists of two charges of equal magnitude but opposite sign separated by a distance d.
The potential due to a dipole: V = (1 / 4πε₀) * (p * cosθ / r²).
The electric field due to a dipole: Er = (1 / 4πε₀) * (2p * cosθ / r³) along the axis, and Eθ = (1 / 4πε₀) * (p * sinθ / r³) perpendicular to the axis.

flashcards.title: Capacitance of a Capacitor
explanation: Capacitance (C) is the ability of a system to store charge per unit potential difference.
For parallel plate capacitors: C = (ε₀ * A) / d, where A is the plate area and d is the separation.
For a spherical capacitor: C = 4πε₀ * (ab / (b - a)), where a and b are radii of inner and outer spheres.

flashcards.title: Energy Stored in a Capacitor and Forces
explanation: Energy stored in a capacitor: E = (1 / 2) * C * V², representing the energy due to the electric field between the plates.
Force between plates of a capacitor: F = Q² / (2 * ε₀ * A).
Surface charge density (σ): Charge per unit area of the capacitor plates, given by σ = Q / A.

flashcards.title: Electromotive Force and Electric Current
explanation: Electromotive Force (EMF): The total energy per unit charge when the cell is open and not supplying current.
Electric Current (I): The rate of flow of electric charge, given by I = q / t, where q is charge and t is time.

flashcards.title: Drift Velocity and Resistivity
explanation: Drift Velocity (v_d): The velocity of electrons in a conductor, given by v_d = I / (n * e * A), where n is the number of electrons per unit volume, e is the charge of an electron, and A is the cross-sectional area.
Resistivity (ρ): The intrinsic property of a material resisting current, given by ρ = m / (n * e² * τ), where m is electron mass and τ is relaxation time.

flashcards.title: Ohm's Law and Resistance
explanation: Ohm's Law: Voltage across a conductor is directly proportional to current through it, given by V = I * R.
Resistance (R): Depends on material resistivity (ρ), length (L), and cross-sectional area (A), given by R = ρ * (L / A).
For resistors in parallel, the equivalent resistance is given by 1 / R = 1 / R₁ + 1 / R₂ + ....

flashcards.title: Power, Temperature Effects, and Kirchhoff's Laws
formulas: P = V * I = I² * R = V² / R
explanation: Electrical Power (P): The rate at which electrical energy is consumed, given by P = V * I = I² * R = V² / R.
Variation of Resistance: Resistance changes with temperature, given by R = R₀ * (1 + α * (T - T₀)).
Kirchhoff's First Law: The algebraic sum of currents at any junction is zero.
Kirchhoff's Second Law: The algebraic sum of voltage drops and EMFs in a closed loop is zero.

flashcards.title: Biot-Savart Law and Magnetic Field
explanation: Biot-Savart Law: Magnetic field (dB) at a point due to current element is proportional to current and inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
Magnetic Field due to Long Straight Current-Carrying Conductor: B = (μ₀ * I) / (2πr).
Magnetic Field at Center of Circular Loop: B = (μ₀ * I) / (2r).
Magnetic Field at Center of a Coil with n Turns: B = (μ₀ * n * I) / (2r).

flashcards.title: Magnetic Field in Special Cases
formulas: B = μ₀ * n * I (inside straight solenoid)
explanation: Magnetic Field on Axis of Circular Loop: Depends on distance (x) from the center and radius (r).
Magnetic Field Inside a Toroidal Solenoid: B = μ₀ * n * I.
Magnetic Field Inside a Straight Solenoid: Uniform and parallel to the solenoid's axis, given by B = μ₀ * n * I.

flashcards.title: Force and Torque on Current-Carrying Conductors
explanation: Force on Moving Charge in a Magnetic Field: F = q(v × B), perpendicular to both velocity (v) and magnetic field (B).
Force on Current-Carrying Conductor: F = I(l × B), where l is the conductor length.
Force Between Two Parallel Wires: Attractive or repulsive force depends on the direction of currents in the wires.
Torque on a Current-Carrying Loop: τ = m × B, where m is the magnetic moment.

flashcards.title: Magnetic Dipole and Energy
explanation: Magnetic Dipole Moment: For a current loop, m = q(2a), where q is pole strength and 2a is the length of the dipole.
Potential Energy of a Magnetic Dipole: U = -mBcosθ, depends on the angle between m and B.
Torque on a Magnetic Dipole: τ = m × B, perpendicular to both m and B.

flashcards.title: Gauss's Law for Magnetism
explanation: Gauss's Law for Magnetic Fields: The net magnetic flux through any closed Gaussian surface is zero, as magnetic monopoles do not exist.

flashcards.title: Magnetic Dipole Moments
explanation: Spin Magnetic Dipole Moment (μ_s): Depends on the spin angular momentum (S) of electrons.
Orbital Magnetic Dipole Moment (μ_l): Depends on the orbital angular momentum (L) of electrons.

flashcards.title: Magnetic Properties of Materials
explanation: Diamagnetism: Materials develop a weak magnetization in a direction opposite to the applied magnetic field.
Paramagnetism: Materials have unpaired electrons and develop weak magnetization in the direction of the magnetic field.
Ferromagnetism: Materials exhibit strong magnetization in the direction of the magnetic field due to domain alignment.

flashcards.title: Maxwell's Extension of Ampere's Law
explanation: Maxwell's Extension: A changing electric field produces a magnetic field, given by the equation ∮B · ds = μ₀ε₀(dp/dt).

flashcards.title: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law
explanation: Magnetic Flux (Φ): The product of the magnetic field (B), area (A), and the cosine of the angle (θ) between them. Measured in Weber.
Faraday's Law: The induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux through a coil.
For a coil with N turns: e = -N(dΦ/dt).

flashcards.title: Lenz's Law and Self Induction
explanation: Lenz's Law: The direction of the induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it.
Self Induction: The phenomenon of inducing an EMF in a coil due to a change in its own current.
Inductance (L): For N turns, L = NΦ / i, where Φ is the flux and i is the current.

flashcards.title: Series RL Circuit and Magnetic Energy
explanation: Series RL Circuit: The rise of current in an RL circuit is given by i = (e / R) * (1 - e^(-t/τ)), where τ = L / R is the time constant.
Magnetic Energy: Energy stored in an inductor's magnetic field is U = (1/2) * L * I².

flashcards.title: Mutual Induction and Magnetic Energy Density
explanation: Mutual Induction: The phenomenon of inducing EMF in one coil due to a change in current in a neighboring coil, given by e₂ = -M(di₁/dt) and e₁ = -M(di₂/dt).
Magnetic Energy Density (u): Energy stored per unit volume in a magnetic field, given by u = B² / (2μ₀).

flashcards.title: Basics of Alternating Current
explanation: Alternating Current: Its magnitude changes periodically and reverses direction. Represented as I = I₀sinωt, where I₀ is the peak value.
Mean Value of A.C.: The average current over a cycle is Iₘ = 2I₀ / π.
RMS Value: The root mean square current is Iᵣₘₛ = I₀ / √2.

flashcards.title: AC through Resistor, Inductor, and Capacitor
explanation: A.C. through Resistor: The EMF is in phase with the current.
A.C. through Inductor: The EMF leads the current by a phase angle of π/2. Inductive reactance is Xₗ = ωL.
A.C. through Capacitor: The EMF lags the current by a phase angle of π/2. Capacitive reactance is Xc = 1 / ωC.

flashcards.title: Impedance and A.C. Circuits
explanation: For Series LR Circuit: Impedance Z = √(R² + (ωL)²).
For Series CR Circuit: Impedance Z = √(R² + (1 / ωC)²).
For Series LCR Circuit: The phase angle ϕ is given by tanϕ = (ωL - 1 / ωC) / R.

flashcards.title: Power and Transformers
explanation: Power in A.C. Circuit: Average power is Pₐᵥ = Iᵣₘₛ²R = EᵣₘₛIᵣₘₛcosϕ, where ϕ is the power factor.
Transformer Voltage: The ratio of secondary to primary voltage is Vₛ / Vₚ = Nₛ / Nₚ.
Transformer Current: The ratio of secondary to primary current is Iₛ / Iₚ = Nₚ / Nₛ.

flashcards.title: Conduction and Displacement Currents
explanation: Conduction Current: Current due to the flow of electrons through conducting wires in an electric circuit.
Displacement Current (Iₚ): Arises due to the time rate of change of electric flux in a part of the circuit, given by Iₚ = ε₀(dΦₑ / dt).

flashcards.title: Modified Ampere's Circuital Law
explanation: Ampere's Circuital Law (Modified): The total magnetic field around a closed loop is due to both conduction current (Ic) and displacement current (Iₚ).

flashcards.title: Maxwell's Equations
explanation: Gauss's Law in Electrostatics: The electric flux through a closed surface is proportional to the enclosed charge.
Gauss's Law in Magnetism: The net magnetic flux through a closed surface is zero.
Faraday's Law of Induction: The induced EMF is equal to the negative rate of change of magnetic flux.
Ampere-Maxwell Law: Relates magnetic fields to both conduction and displacement currents.

flashcards.title: Velocity of EM Waves in Free Space
explanation: The speed of electromagnetic waves in free space is given by v = 1 / √(ε₀μ₀) and is approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

flashcards.title: Laws of Reflection and Refraction
formulas: Angle of Incidence = Angle of Reflection
explanation: Laws of Reflection: The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie on the same plane. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

Laws of Refraction (Snell's Law): The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant for two media. Mathematically, sin(i) / sin(r) = μ₂ / μ₁, where μ₂ and μ₁ are refractive indices of the two media.

flashcards.title: Mirror and Lens Formulas
explanation: Mirror Formula: Relates the focal length (f), object distance (u), and image distance (v).
Magnification (m): The ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, given by m = -v / u.

flashcards.title: Spherical Refracting Surfaces and Lenses
explanation: Power of a Spherical Surface (P): Depends on the refractive indices of the two media and the radius of curvature (R).
Lens Maker's Formula: Relates focal length (f) of a lens to its radii of curvature (R₁, R₂) and refractive index (μ).

flashcards.title: Thin Lenses and Optical Instruments
explanation: For Thin Lenses in Contact: The equivalent power (P) is the sum of individual powers of the lenses, P = P₁ + P₂.
Magnification of Combined Lenses: The total magnification is the product of individual magnifications, m = m₁ * m₂.
Spherical Aberration: The inability of lenses to focus all rays to a single point, causing a blurry image.

flashcards.title: Huygens' Principle and Interference
explanation: Huygens' Principle: Each point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, spreading in all directions.
Condition for Maximum Intensity: φ = 2nπ or x = nλ.
Condition for Minimum Intensity: φ = (2n + 1)π or x = (2n + 1)λ / 2.
Ratio of Maximum to Minimum Intensity: Given by Iₘₐₓ / Iₘᵢₙ = (a + a')² / (a - a')², where a and a' are amplitudes of the interfering waves.

flashcards.title: Fringe Position and Angular Position
explanation: Position of nth Bright Fringe: yₙ = nλD / d.
Angular Position of nth Bright Fringe: θₙ = nλ / d.
Position of nth Dark Fringe: y'ₙ = (2n + 1)λD / (2d).
Angular Position of nth Dark Fringe: θ'ₙ = (2n + 1)λ / (2d).
Fringe Width: β = λD / d.

flashcards.title: Diffraction of Light
explanation: Single Slit Diffraction: Condition for dark fringes is sinθ = nλ / a, where n = ±1, ±2, ±3, ....
Width of Central Maximum: θₘ = 2λD / a, where D is the distance between slit and screen, and a is slit width.
Grating: Maxima occur at angles θ where sinθ = nλ.

flashcards.title: Polarisation and Laws
explanation: Brewster's Law: μ = tan(p), where μ is the refractive index of the medium, and p is the angle of polarisation.
Law of Malus: I = I₀ cos²θ, where I₀ is the intensity of incident light, and θ is the angle between the polariser and analyser.

chapters.name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

flashcards.title: Energy of a Photon and Photoelectric Effect
explanation: Energy of a Photon: E = hν, where h is Planck's constant and ν is the frequency of light.
Photoelectric Effect: The energy of incident light is used to overcome the work function (φ) and impart kinetic energy to the ejected electron.
Work Function: φ = hν₀, where ν₀ is the threshold frequency for the metal.

flashcards.title: Compton Effect and de Broglie Wavelength
explanation: Compton Effect: Describes the change in wavelength (λ' - λ) of X-rays scattered by a material, where λ_c = h / (mₑc) is the Compton wavelength.
de Broglie Wavelength: The wavelength of matter waves is given by λ = h / mv, where m is mass and v is velocity.

flashcards.title: Wave and Group Velocity
explanation: Wave Equation: The displacement of a wave is given by y = A cos2π(vt - x / λ).
Phase Velocity (vₚ): The velocity of the wave phase is vₚ = ω / k.
Group Velocity (vₛ): The velocity of the wave group or packet is vₛ = dω / dk.

flashcards.title: Uncertainty Principle
explanation: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle: It is impossible to precisely measure both the position and momentum (ΔxΔp) of a particle simultaneously.
Uncertainty in Energy and Time: The uncertainty in energy (ΔE) and time (Δt) is related by ΔEΔt ≥ h / 4π.

flashcards.title: Velocity and Energy of an Electron
explanation: Velocity of Electron in an Orbit: v = e / √(4πε₀m r), where r is the radius of the orbit, e is charge, m is mass, and ε₀ is permittivity.
Total Energy of Hydrogen Atom: E = -e² / (8πε₀r), indicating that energy is inversely proportional to the orbit radius.

flashcards.title: Atomic Spectra and Rydberg Formula
explanation: Atomic Spectra: Emission or absorption lines are due to electron transitions between energy levels.
Rydberg Formula: 1 / λ = R (1 / n₁² - 1 / n₂²), where R is the Rydberg constant and n₁ < n₂.
Lyman Series: Transitions to n₁ = 1.
Balmer Series: Transitions to n₁ = 2.
Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund Series: Transitions to n₁ = 3, 4, and 5, respectively.

flashcards.title: Orbital Wavelength and Stability
explanation: Orbital Wavelength (Bohr Model): λ = h / e √(4πε₀r / m), where h is Planck's constant.
Condition for Orbital Stability: nλ = 2πr, where n is the orbit number and r is the orbit radius.

flashcards.title: Orbital Radii in Bohr Atom
explanation: Orbital Radii: The radius of the nth orbit in a hydrogen atom is given by rₙ = n²h²ε₀ / (πme²), where n is the orbit number.

flashcards.title: Atomic Properties
explanation: Atomic Mass Unit (u): Defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. 1 u = 1.66054 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931 MeV.
Nuclear Radius: R = R₀A^(1/3), where R₀ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, and A is the mass number.

flashcards.title: Nuclear Density and Forces
explanation: Nuclear Density (ρ): The density of a nucleus is given by ρ = (A × mₙ) / (4/3πR³), where A is the mass number, mₙ is the mass of a nucleon, and R is the nuclear radius.
Nuclear Radius: R = R₀A^(1/3), where R₀ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
Nuclear Forces: Short-range attractive forces that hold nucleons together, overcoming the repulsion between protons.

flashcards.title: Mass Defect and Binding Energy
explanation: Mass Defect (Δm): The difference between the mass of the nucleus and the sum of its nucleons.
Binding Energy (BE): Energy equivalent to the mass defect, given by BE = Δmc².
Binding Energy per Nucleon: BE/A, represents the stability of a nucleus.

flashcards.title: Radioactivity and Decay Laws
explanation: Radioactive Decay Law: The number of undecayed nuclei (N) decreases exponentially over time, given by N = N₀e⁻λt.
Half-Life (T): The time taken for half the nuclei to decay, T = ln(2) / λ.
Average Life (Tₐᵥ): The mean lifetime of a radioactive nucleus, Tₐᵥ = 1 / λ.
